summary.title: How to create software quality.
summary.one_liner: Software quality practices only work in the context they were designed for, so you should model your problem domain's complexity and where feedback happens before choosing a technique.
keywords: john ousterhout philosophy of software design
takeaways: Quality techniques such as incremental rollouts depend on context: they help with high-volume, consistent usage and help little with low-volume or highly varied usage.
Classify complexity as essential domain, scale, or accidental, since each calls for different quality approaches.
Feedback inside the development loop creates quality faster than feedback across release iterations, which mainly measures quality.
Developer-led testing creates quality within the local loop, while QA-led testing measures quality and influences later iterations.
Read the author's related reading list (Ousterhout, Brooks, Michelle Bu, Hillel Wayne's TLA+, Domain-Driven Design) to dig deeper.
summary.summary: The author argues that software quality is context specific, and that playbooks such as automated rollouts, A/B testing, or heterogeneous redundant implementations work only in the environments they came from. He proposes classifying complexity into essential domain, scale, and accidental types, and notes that team maturity and problem domain shape the right approach. He builds on a loop model, separating fast feedback inside the development loop (which creates quality) from slower production and QA feedback (which mostly measures it). The post ends with a reading list including works by Ousterhout, Brooks, Michelle Bu, Hillel Wayne, and Vernon.
